tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

level.description: Effort level the review ran at

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

short_summary.description: Compressed label for compact UI (≤60 chars): the claim alone, no rationale or consequence clause

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

verdict.description: Set when a verify pass ran; absent on inline-only reviews

outcome.description: Set ONLY when re-reporting after applying fixes: what happened to this finding

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

> Source: [src/main/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt](../../../../../src/main/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt) · Last synced with code: 2026-09-27

## Role

The data-access layer for inventory, written by Robert. It is the only class that talks to the
`inventory` table (created by [V1__create_inventory.sql](../resources/db/migration/V1__create_inventory.sql.md)).
Request flow for both reads: controller → service → **repository** → Postgres. `findAll` serves
`GET /inventory` and `findBySkuId` serves `GET /inventory/{skuId}`. Each row comes back as an
`InventoryItem`. The repository only reports what the table holds. It never decides what a missing
row *means* for the API; that's the [service's](InventoryService.kt.md) job. [InventoryRepositoryTest](../../test/inventory/InventoryRepositoryTest.kt.md)
checks it against a real Postgres.

Robert's own summary, written while he worked on it:

> The class initializes the JDBC client, which allows us to make SQL queries. `findAll` has the
> return type `List<InventoryItem>`: we query the database for all entries and order them
> alphabetically by `sku_id`. We are explicit in the query with the result-set lambda so that
> Kotlin knows we are getting inventory items and each item is non-null. Otherwise Kotlin won't
> compile, because we haven't dealt with the null case.

## Walkthrough

### Imports

```kotlin
import org.springframework.jdbc.core.simple.JdbcClient
import org.springframework.stereotype.Repository
```

**Kotlin:** Kotlin imports `kotlin.*` automatically (like Java's `java.lang`), and classes in the
same package need no import, which is why `InventoryItem` has none. Everything from a library,
Spring included, has to be imported.

### A Spring bean with constructor injection

```kotlin
/** Reads inventory rows from Postgres, used by the service layer. */
@Repository
class InventoryRepository(
    private val jdbcClient: JdbcClient,
){
```

**Kotlin:** the parentheses after the class name are the **primary constructor**. `private val`
in front of a parameter declares a property and assigns it in one step. The Java equivalent is a
`private final JdbcClient jdbcClient;` field plus a constructor that sets it. `private` because
nothing outside the repository should reach into its database handle. `val` because the reference
never changes.

The **trailing comma** after the last parameter is optional. Kotlin style recommends it when each
item sits on its own line: adding a second parameter later then changes one line in the diff
instead of two, and lines can be reordered without fixing commas. Java allows this in array
initializers but not in parameter lists.

**Kotlin (KDoc):** `/** ... */` is **KDoc**, Kotlin's Javadoc. It belongs to the declaration
*directly* below it (annotations may sit in between, but a blank line or another comment
detaches it). The editor shows it when you hover over the class or function anywhere in the
project. It answers "what does this do?" for the caller. A `// Why:` comment answers "why is it
built this way?" for whoever changes the file, and the editor ignores it. The project's
[check_kdoc.py](../../../../../scripts/check_kdoc.py) requires KDoc on every non-private declaration.

**Spring:** two separate things happen here.
1. **Bean creation.** At startup, `@SpringBootApplication` scans its package and every package
   below it for classes with a stereotype annotation: `@Component`, or one of its specialized
   forms, `@Repository`, `@Service` and `@RestController`. `@Repository` is what makes Spring create
   an `InventoryRepository` in the running app. Without it, the service can't be injected, and the
   app fails to start with `NoSuchBeanDefinitionException`. The test doesn't need the annotation,
   because `@Import(InventoryRepository::class)` registers the class by hand. That's why the test
   alone can't prove the annotation is there. The full-context controller test does.
   `@Repository` rather than a plain `@Component` because it names the class's role: data access.
2. **Constructor injection.** Spring sees that the class has a single constructor, and fills in its
   parameters with matching beans. No `@Autowired` is needed for a single constructor. The test
   class needs `@Autowired` because JUnit creates it, not Spring. The `JdbcClient` bean itself
   comes from Spring Boot's auto-configuration, which builds a `DataSource` from the datasource
   settings and a `JdbcClient` on top of it. Beans are created at startup, so a missing dependency
   fails fast instead of on the first request.

**Spring (exception translation):** `JdbcClient` already turns `SQLException`s into Spring's
`DataAccessException` hierarchy (see the backstop test's `DataIntegrityViolationException`).
For JDBC code, `@Repository` is mostly about bean creation and naming the role.

### `findAll`: the function signature

```kotlin
/** Returns every SKU with its quantity, sorted by SKU id; zero-stock SKUs included, empty list when none. */
fun findAll(): List<InventoryItem> = jdbcClient.sql("SELECT sku_id, quantity FROM inventory ORDER BY sku_id")
```

**Kotlin:** a function is `fun name(params): ReturnType`. Parameters are written `name: Type`,
the reverse of Java, and the return type comes after the parentheses. `findAll` takes no
parameters. No modifier means `public`, which is what the service needs
([public by default](../../test/inventory/InventoryRepositoryTest.kt.md)).

`List<InventoryItem>` is a generic type, as in Java. Two Kotlin differences:
- **`List` is read-only.** It has no `add` or `remove`. A changeable list is a `MutableList`. The
  caller gets a snapshot it can't modify.
- **No `?`, so never null.** The compiler won't let this function return `null`. That's how the
  "empty list, never null" test is guaranteed by the type, not just by the implementation.

**Kotlin (expression body):** `= expression` instead of `{ ... return ... }`. The whole body is one
call chain, so its result is the return value. Robert first wrote a block body with a local `val`
and `return`, and shortened it once it passed. Concept explained in full in
[TestcontainersConfiguration.kt](../../test/support/TestcontainersConfiguration.kt.md#the-container-bean).

**SQL:**
- `SELECT sku_id, quantity` names the columns instead of `SELECT *`. The row mapper below reads
  those two columns by name, so the query states exactly what the mapper depends on. A column
  added later can't silently change what the query returns.
- `ORDER BY sku_id`: without `ORDER BY`, SQL guarantees **no** order. Postgres returns rows in
  whatever order is cheapest, which can change after updates, deletes or a new query plan. The
  decision (2026-09-24) was to sort by SKU id so every response is deterministic. `sku_id` is
  `TEXT`, so the order is by text, not numeric. Postgres sorts text by the database's **collation**
  (its sorting rules), so uppercase, lowercase and digits don't always follow a plain A-Z order.
  The rule we promise is simply "ordered by `sku_id`". The test inserts SKUs out of order to prove it.
- Column names are the **database** names (`sku_id`, snake_case), not the Kotlin property
  names (`skuId`).

**Spring:** `jdbcClient.sql(...)` only *prepares* a statement. Nothing runs until a terminal
call such as `.list()`:

| Step | What it does | Touches the database? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `.sql("SELECT ...")` | stores the SQL text | no |
| `.query { ... }` | stores the recipe for turning **one row** into an `InventoryItem` | no |
| `.list()` | runs the query, applies the recipe to each row, collects the results | **yes** |

`.query` doesn't work on results; it's handed over *before* the query runs.

### Mapping each row: the lambda

```kotlin
fun findAll(): List<InventoryItem> = jdbcClient.sql("SELECT sku_id, quantity FROM inventory ORDER BY sku_id")

// Why: Chose the result set lambda instead of InventoryItem::class.java so Kotlin sees the items as non null.
        .query { rs, _ ->
            InventoryItem(rs.getString("sku_id"), rs.getInt("quantity"))
        }
        .list()
```

**Kotlin (lambdas):** `{ rs, _ -> ... }` is a **lambda**, a function written inline. Parameters go
left of `->` and the result goes right. The last expression is the return value, with no `return`.
- `rs` is only a name (short for `ResultSet`, the JDBC convention). `row` would work just as well.
- `_` means "there's a parameter here, and I don't use it". Spring's `RowMapper` always passes
  two arguments (the result set and the row number), so the lambda must accept two. `_` has
  nothing to do with looping: `.list()` does the looping and calls the lambda once per row.
- **The lambda returns a value on every call.** Its last expression, `InventoryItem(...)`, is the
  return value, and `.list()` collects those return values into the list. Without them there would
  be nothing to collect. It's the same shape as `map` on a plain list:

  ```kotlin
  val books = listOf(Book("Dune", 1965), Book("Emma", 1815))
  val titles = books.map { book -> book.title.uppercase() }   // ["DUNE", "EMMA"]
  ```

  | Call | Input | Return value |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 1 | `Book("Dune", 1965)` / row `('a-sku', 5)` | `"DUNE"` / `InventoryItem("a-sku", 5)` |
  | 2 | `Book("Emma", 1815)` / row `('b-sku', 0)` | `"EMMA"` / `InventoryItem("b-sku", 0)` |

  Only what the lambda returns reaches the result: `{ book -> book.year }` would give
  `[1965, 1815]`, a `List<Int>`, and the titles would be gone.
- The types are inferred from `RowMapper`, so you never write `rs: ResultSet`.
- **Trailing lambda:** when a lambda is the last argument, it moves outside the parentheses, and
  when it's the only one, the parentheses disappear, so `.query { ... }` instead of `.query({ ... })`.
  See [trailing lambdas](../../build.gradle.kts.md#the-file-is-kotlin-trailing-lambdas).
- **SAM conversion:** `RowMapper` is a Java interface with a single abstract method. Kotlin lets a
  lambda stand in for it. In Java you'd write the lambda `(rs, rowNum) -> new InventoryItem(...)`.

**JDBC:** `rs.getString("sku_id")` and `rs.getInt("quantity")` read the current row's columns by
database name. Every name here must appear in the `SELECT`, or it fails at runtime with "column
not found". Reading by position (`getInt(2)`) also works, but breaks silently if the `SELECT` is
reordered.

**Why a hand-written lambda and not `query(InventoryItem::class.java)`:** Robert's first version
used the class-based mapping, and it didn't compile:

```
Return type mismatch: expected 'List<InventoryItem>', actual '(Mutable)List<InventoryItem?>'.
```

Spring 7 annotates its Java API with JSpecify nullability annotations, and Kotlin reads them
(see [platform types](../../build.gradle.kts.md#compiler-options)). In spring-jdbc 7.0.9:

```java
<T> MappedQuerySpec<@Nullable T> query(Class<T> mappedClass);
<T extends @Nullable Object> MappedQuerySpec<T> query(RowMapper<T> rowMapper);
```

- The class-based version is declared as "each row *might* map to null", because it also handles
  single-column queries where the value can be SQL `NULL`. So Kotlin sees `InventoryItem?`.
- The row-mapper version keeps the lambda's own return type. The lambda always builds a real
  `InventoryItem`, so the list is `List<InventoryItem>`.

The fix works at **compile time**: the class-based mapping would never actually have returned null
for these rows, but the compiler couldn't prove it. The compiler never looks at the database, so it
can't know `sku_id` is a primary key; it only reads Spring's declared types. The non-null columns
matter at *runtime* instead (see "Null safety, one level deeper" below). It's also more explicit, since you can see
which column goes into which property. That fits the reason `JdbcClient` was chosen (explicit SQL).

`(Mutable)List` is Kotlin saying it can't tell whether a Java `List` is meant to be changed. It's
harmless, because it fits a read-only `List` return type.

**Null safety, one level deeper:** `rs.getString(...)` is a Java method, so its result is a
platform type (`String!`). If it were ever null, Kotlin would throw when passing it into
`InventoryItem`'s non-null `skuId`. That can't happen: `sku_id` is the primary key, and a primary
key is never NULL. The migration's constraints back up the Kotlin types.

**Spring:** `.list()` runs the query, calls the lambda once per row, and collects the results. No
rows means an empty list, never null.

**Kotlin (a comment in the middle of a chain):** the `// Why:` comment and the blank line sit
*inside* the expression, between `.sql(...)` and `.query`. That still compiles: a line that starts
with `.` continues the expression above it, and comments and blank lines in between are ignored.
The comment sits next to the part of the chain it explains.

### `findBySkuId`: a nullable return type

```kotlin
/** Returns a SKU with its quantity for a specific SKU. Will return null if no such SKU exists */
fun findBySkuId(skuId: String): InventoryItem? = jdbcClient.sql("SELECT sku_id, quantity FROM inventory WHERE sku_id = :skuId")
```

**Kotlin (nullable types):** the `?` in `InventoryItem?` is part of the type. `InventoryItem`
means "always an item". `InventoryItem?` means "an item or `null`". They are two different types, and
the compiler keeps them apart:
- You can't call `.quantity` on an `InventoryItem?` without first dealing with the `null` case
  (`?.`, `?:`, an `if (x != null)` check, or `!!`).
- You can't return `null` from a function declared as `InventoryItem`, or pass an `InventoryItem?`
  where an `InventoryItem` is expected.

In Java every object reference can be null and nothing warns you. The nearest Java habit is
returning `Optional<InventoryItem>`. Kotlin puts that information in the type itself, at no cost:
an `InventoryItem?` is just a normal reference at runtime, with no wrapper object.

**Why nullable and not an exception here:** "no row" is an ordinary answer to a lookup, not a
failure. The repository says "nothing there" with `null`, and the service decides that, for this
endpoint, nothing there means `404`. The purchase endpoint will make the same lookup and give its own
answer. The repository test `findBySkuId returns null for a missing SKU` pins this down.

**SQL:** `WHERE sku_id = :skuId` compares text exactly, so `widget` and `WIDGET` are different
SKUs (the case-sensitivity decision in the README's contract-gaps row). `:skuId` is a **named
parameter**: a placeholder, not the value. It is filled in by the `.param(...)` call below.

### Binding the parameter and mapping the row

```kotlin
// Why: We parameterized the skuid instead of adding it directly to the sql above for sql injection prevention.
        .param("skuId", skuId)
        .query{rs, _ ->
            InventoryItem(skuId = rs.getString("sku_id"), quantity = rs.getInt("quantity"))
        }
```

**Spring (`.param`):** `.param("skuId", skuId)` binds the Kotlin value to the `:skuId` placeholder.
`JdbcClient` turns `:skuId` into JDBC's `?` and sends the value separately from the SQL text, as
a `PreparedStatement` parameter. The database parses the SQL first and only then receives the value,
so the value can never become part of the SQL.

**Why (SQL injection):** building the SQL with a string template instead,
`"... WHERE sku_id = '$skuId'"`, would let a request for the SKU `x' OR '1'='1` rewrite the query.
The SKU comes straight from the URL, so it's untrusted input. Binding it as a parameter
makes any SKU, however strange, just a string to compare. Named parameters (`:skuId`) instead of
positional ones (`?`) are a readability choice: the name says which value goes where. The
`.param` call also accepts a position, `.param(1, skuId)`, for `?` placeholders.

**Kotlin (named arguments):** `InventoryItem(skuId = ..., quantity = ...)` names each constructor
argument, where `findAll` passes them by position. Both compile to the same call. Named arguments
make it impossible to swap two values of compatible types and can be in any order. Concept explained in
[TestcontainersConfiguration.kt](../../test/support/TestcontainersConfiguration.kt.md#testconfigurationproxybeanmethods--false).

The lambda is the same row mapper as in `findAll` (see [the lambda](#mapping-each-row-the-lambda)).
`.query{` without a space is legal, and it formats the same.

### `singleOrNull`: zero or one row

```kotlin
// Why: The list singleOrNull below, we did this over the Java optional so we can stay within kotlin. We wont have more than one entry in the list because sku_id is the primary key so it is unique.
        .list().singleOrNull()
```

**Kotlin (`singleOrNull`):** a standard-library function on any `List`. It returns the only
element if the list has exactly one, and `null` otherwise:

| List | `singleOrNull()` | `single()` | `firstOrNull()` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `[]` | `null` | throws `NoSuchElementException` | `null` |
| `[a]` | `a` | `a` | `a` |
| `[a, b]` | **`null`** | throws `IllegalArgumentException` | `a` |

Note the last row: with two elements, `singleOrNull()` returns `null` silently. It doesn't
throw. So if two rows could ever match, the SKU would be reported as missing. That can't happen here
for the reason in the `// Why:` comment: `sku_id` is the primary key, so the database never holds two
rows with the same SKU. As with `findAll`, the migration's constraints are what make the Kotlin code
correct.

**Why not `JdbcClient`'s own `.optional()`:** the query spec also has `.optional()`, which returns a
Java `Optional<InventoryItem>`. Kotlin code would then convert it with `.orElse(null)` or
`.getOrNull()`. `.list().singleOrNull()` gets `InventoryItem?` directly, and a nullable type is the
Kotlin way to say "maybe absent". `.single()` was ruled out because it throws on no rows, and no rows
is a normal answer here.

**Kotlin (why the return type works):** `.list()` returns `List<InventoryItem>` (non-null items,
thanks to the lambda), and `singleOrNull()` on a `List<T>` returns `T?`. That gives
`InventoryItem?`, which matches the declared return type.

## Check your understanding

- What does `@Repository` do that `@Import(InventoryRepository::class)` does in the test? Why does the running app need the annotation?
- Where does the `JdbcClient` passed to the constructor come from? Why is there no `@Autowired`?
- Why is `jdbcClient` a `private val` rather than a plain constructor parameter or a `var`?
- What is the difference between the KDoc above `findAll` and the `// Why:` comment? Who reads each one, and where?
- Why does `query(InventoryItem::class.java)` produce `List<InventoryItem?>`, while the lambda produces `List<InventoryItem>`?
- What would the API return if `ORDER BY sku_id` were removed? Would the test notice every time?
- Why is it `getString("sku_id")` and not `getString("skuId")`?
- The expression body has no `return`. What makes that allowed?
- If `sku_id` could be NULL in the database, what would happen at runtime, and where?
- The service calls `findBySkuId("x' OR '1'='1")`. What SQL reaches Postgres, and what comes back?
- If the primary key were dropped and two `widget` rows existed, what would `findBySkuId("widget")` return? What would the API answer?
- Why can the service call `findBySkuId(skuId).quantity` only after handling `null`? Which line of the service does that?

instead of two, and lines can be reordered without fixing commas. Java allows this in array
initializers but not in parameter lists.

**Kotlin (KDoc):** `/** ... */` is **KDoc**, Kotlin's Javadoc. It belongs to the declaration
*directly* below it (annotations may sit in between, but a blank line or another comment
detaches it). The editor shows it when you hover over the class or function anywhere in the
project. It answers "what does this do?" for the caller. A `// Why:` comment answers "why is it
built this way?" for whoever changes the file, and the editor ignores it. The project's
[check_kdoc.py](../../../../../scripts/check_kdoc.py) requires KDoc on every non-private declaration.

**Spring:** two separate things happen here.
1. **Bean creation.** At startup, `@SpringBootApplication` scans its package and every package
   below it for classes with a stereotype annotation: `@Component`, or one of its specialized
   forms, `@Repository`, `@Service` and `@RestController`. `@Repository` is what makes Spring create
   an `InventoryRepository` in the running app. Without it, the service can't be injected, and the
   app fails to start with `NoSuchBeanDefinitionException`. The test doesn't need the annotation,
   because `@Import(InventoryRepository::class)` registers the class by hand. That's why the test
   alone can't prove the annotation is there. The full-context controller test does.
   `@Repository` rather than a plain `@Component` because it names the class's role: data access.
2. **Constructor injection.** Spring sees that the class has a single constructor, and fills in its
   parameters with matching beans. No `@Autowired` is needed for a single constructor. The test
   class needs `@Autowired` because JUnit creates it, not Spring. The `JdbcClient` bean itself
   comes from Spring Boot's auto-configuration, which builds a `DataSource` from the datasource
   settings and a `JdbcClient` on top of it. Beans are created at startup, so a missing dependency
   fails fast instead of on the first request.

**Spring (exception translation):** `JdbcClient` already turns `SQLException`s into Spring's
`DataAccessException` hierarchy (see the backstop test's `DataIntegrityViolationException`).
For JDBC code, `@Repository` is mostly about bean creation and naming the role.

### `findAll`: the function signature

```kotlin
/** Returns every SKU with its quantity, sorted by SKU id; zero-stock SKUs included, empty list when none. */
fun findAll(): List<InventoryItem> = jdbcClient.sql("SELECT sku_id, quantity FROM inventory ORDER BY sku_id")
```

**Kotlin:** a function is `fun name(params): ReturnType`. Parameters are written `name: Type`,
the reverse of Java, and the return type comes after the parentheses. `findAll` takes no
parameters. No modifier means `public`, which is what the service needs
([public by default](../../test/inventory/InventoryRepositoryTest.kt.md)).

`List<InventoryItem>` is a generic type, as in Java. Two Kotlin differences:
- **`List` is read-only.** It has no `add` or `remove`. A changeable list is a `MutableList`. The
  caller gets a snapshot it can't modify.
- **No `?`, so never null.** The compiler won't let this function return `null`. That's how the
  "empty list, never null" test is guaranteed by the type, not just by the implementation.

**Kotlin (expression body):** `= expression` instead of `{ ... return ... }`. The whole body is one
call chain, so its result is the return value. Robert first wrote a block body with a local `val`
and `return`, and shortened it once it passed. Concept explained in full in
[TestcontainersConfiguration.kt](../../test/support/TestcontainersConfiguration.kt.md#the-container-bean).

**SQL:**
- `SELECT sku_id, quantity` names the columns instead of `SELECT *`. The row mapper below reads
  those two columns by name, so the query states exactly what the mapper depends on. A column
  added later can't silently change what the query returns.
- `ORDER BY sku_id`: without `ORDER BY`, SQL guarantees **no** order. Postgres returns rows in
  whatever order is cheapest, which can change after updates, deletes or a new query plan. The
  decision (2026-09-24) was to sort by SKU id so every response is deterministic. `sku_id` is
  `TEXT`, so the order is by text, not numeric. Postgres sorts text by the database's **collation**
  (its sorting rules), so uppercase, lowercase and digits don't always follow a plain A-Z order.
  The rule we promise is simply "ordered by `sku_id`". The test inserts SKUs out of order to prove it.
- Column names are the **database** names (`sku_id`, snake_case), not the Kotlin property
  names (`skuId`).

**Spring:** `jdbcClient.sql(...)` only *prepares* a statement. Nothing runs until a terminal
call such as `.list()`:

| Step | What it does | Touches the database? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `.sql("SELECT ...")` | stores the SQL text | no |
| `.query { ... }` | stores the recipe for turning **one row** into an `InventoryItem` | no |
| `.list()` | runs the query, applies the recipe to each row, collects the results | **yes** |

`.query` doesn't work on results; it's handed over *before* the query runs.

### Mapping each row: the lambda

```kotlin
fun findAll(): List<InventoryItem> = jdbcClient.sql("SELECT sku_id, quantity FROM inventory ORDER BY sku_id")

// Why: Chose the result set lambda instead of InventoryItem::class.java so Kotlin sees the items as non null.
        .query { rs, _ ->
            InventoryItem(rs.getString("sku_id"), rs.getInt("quantity"))
        }
        .list()
```

**Kotlin (lambdas):** `{ rs, _ -> ... }` is a **lambda**, a function written inline. Parameters go
left of `->` and the result goes right. The last expression is the return value, with no `return`.
- `rs` is only a name (short for `ResultSet`, the JDBC convention). `row` would work just as well.
- `_` means "there's a parameter here, and I don't use it". Spring's `RowMapper` always passes
  two arguments (the result set and the row number), so the lambda must accept two. `_` has
  nothing to do with looping: `.list()` does the looping and calls the lambda once per row.
- **The lambda returns a value on every call.** Its last expression, `InventoryItem(...)`, is the
  return value, and `.list()` collects those return values into the list. Without them there would
  be nothing to collect. It's the same shape as `map` on a plain list:

  ```kotlin
  val books = listOf(Book("Dune", 1965), Book("Emma", 1815))
  val titles = books.map { book -> book.title.uppercase() }   // ["DUNE", "EMMA"]
  ```

  | Call | Input | Return value |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 1 | `Book("Dune", 1965)` / row `('a-sku', 5)` | `"DUNE"` / `InventoryItem("a-sku", 5)` |
  | 2 | `Book("Emma", 1815)` / row `('b-sku', 0)` | `"EMMA"` / `InventoryItem("b-sku", 0)` |

  Only what the lambda returns reaches the result: `{ book -> book.year }` would give
  `[1965, 1815]`, a `List<Int>`, and the titles would be gone.
- The types are inferred from `RowMapper`, so you never write `rs: ResultSet`.
- **Trailing lambda:** when a lambda is the last argument, it moves outside the parentheses, and
  when it's the only one, the parentheses disappear, so `.query { ... }` instead of `.query({ ... })`.
  See [trailing lambdas](../../build.gradle.kts.md#the-file-is-kotlin-trailing-lambdas).
- **SAM conversion:** `RowMapper` is a Java interface with a single abstract method. Kotlin lets a
  lambda stand in for it. In Java you'd write the lambda `(rs, rowNum) -> new InventoryItem(...)`.

**JDBC:** `rs.getString("sku_id")` and `rs.getInt("quantity")` read the current row's columns by
database name. Every name here must appear in the `SELECT`, or it fails at runtime with "column
not found". Reading by position (`getInt(2)`) also works, but breaks silently if the `SELECT` is
reordered.

**Why a hand-written lambda and not `query(InventoryItem::class.java)`:** Robert's first version
used the class-based mapping, and it didn't compile:

```
Return type mismatch: expected 'List<InventoryItem>', actual '(Mutable)List<InventoryItem?>'.
```

Spring 7 annotates its Java API with JSpecify nullability annotations, and Kotlin reads them
(see [platform types](../../build.gradle.kts.md#compiler-options)). In spring-jdbc 7.0.9:

```java
<T> MappedQuerySpec<@Nullable T> query(Class<T> mappedClass);
<T extends @Nullable Object> MappedQuerySpec<T> query(RowMapper<T> rowMapper);
```

- The class-based version is declared as "each row *might* map to null", because it also handles
  single-column queries where the value can be SQL `NULL`. So Kotlin sees `InventoryItem?`.
- The row-mapper version keeps the lambda's own return type. The lambda always builds a real
  `InventoryItem`, so the list is `List<InventoryItem>`.

The fix works at **compile time**: the class-based mapping would never actually have returned null
for these rows, but the compiler couldn't prove it. The compiler never looks at the database, so it
can't know `sku_id` is a primary key; it only reads Spring's declared types. The non-null columns
matter at *runtime* instead (see "Null safety, one level deeper" below). It's also more explicit, since you can see
which column goes into which property. That fits the reason `JdbcClient` was chosen (explicit SQL).

`(Mutable)List` is Kotlin saying it can't tell whether a Java `List` is meant to be changed. It's
harmless, because it fits a read-only `List` return type.

**Null safety, one level deeper:** `rs.getString(...)` is a Java method, so its result is a
platform type (`String!`). If it were ever null, Kotlin would throw when passing it into
`InventoryItem`'s non-null `skuId`. That can't happen: `sku_id` is the primary key, and a primary
key is never NULL. The migration's constraints back up the Kotlin types.

**Spring:** `.list()` runs the query, calls the lambda once per row, and collects the results. No
rows means an empty list, never null.

**Kotlin (a comment in the middle of a chain):** the `// Why:` comment and the blank line sit
*inside* the expression, between `.sql(...)` and `.query`. That still compiles: a line that starts
with `.` continues the expression above it, and comments and blank lines in between are ignored.
The comment sits next to the part of the chain it explains.

### `findBySkuId`: a nullable return type

```kotlin
/** Returns a SKU with its quantity for a specific SKU. Will return null if no such SKU exists */
fun findBySkuId(skuId: String): InventoryItem? = jdbcClient.sql("SELECT sku_id, quantity FROM inventory WHERE sku_id = :skuId")
```

**Kotlin (nullable types):** the `?` in `InventoryItem?` is part of the type. `InventoryItem`
means "always an item". `InventoryItem?` means "an item or `null`". They are two different types, and
the compiler keeps them apart:
- You can't call `.quantity` on an `InventoryItem?` without first dealing with the `null` case
  (`?.`, `?:`, an `if (x != null)` check, or `!!`).
- You can't return `null` from a function declared as `InventoryItem`, or pass an `InventoryItem?`
  where an `InventoryItem` is expected.

In Java every object reference can be null and nothing warns you. The nearest Java habit is
returning `Optional<InventoryItem>`. Kotlin puts that information in the type itself, at no cost:
an `InventoryItem?` is just a normal reference at runtime, with no wrapper object.

**Why nullable and not an exception here:** "no row" is an ordinary answer to a lookup, not a
failure. The repository says "nothing there" with `null`, and the service decides that, for this
endpoint, nothing there means `404`. The purchase endpoint will make the same lookup and give its own
answer. The repository test `findBySkuId returns null for a missing SKU` pins this down.

**SQL:** `WHERE sku_id = :skuId` compares text exactly, so `widget` and `WIDGET` are different
SKUs (the case-sensitivity decision in the README's contract-gaps row). `:skuId` is a **named
parameter**: a placeholder, not the value. It is filled in by the `.param(...)` call below.

### Binding the parameter and mapping the row

```kotlin
// Why: We parameterized the skuid instead of adding it directly to the sql above for sql injection prevention.
        .param("skuId", skuId)
        .query{rs, _ ->
            InventoryItem(skuId = rs.getString("sku_id"), quantity = rs.getInt("quantity"))
        }
```

**Spring (`.param`):** `.param("skuId", skuId)` binds the Kotlin value to the `:skuId` placeholder.
`JdbcClient` turns `:skuId` into JDBC's `?` and sends the value separately from the SQL text, as
a `PreparedStatement` parameter. The database parses the SQL first and only then receives the value,
so the value can never become part of the SQL.

**Why (SQL injection):** building the SQL with a string template instead,
`"... WHERE sku_id = '$skuId'"`, would let a request for the SKU `x' OR '1'='1` rewrite the query.
The SKU comes straight from the URL, so it's untrusted input. Binding it as a parameter
makes any SKU, however strange, just a string to compare. Named parameters (`:skuId`) instead of
positional ones (`?`) are a readability choice: the name says which value goes where. The
`.param` call also accepts a position, `.param(1, skuId)`, for `?` placeholders.

**Kotlin (named arguments):** `InventoryItem(skuId = ..., quantity = ...)` names each constructor
argument, where `findAll` passes them by position. Both compile to the same call. Named arguments
make it impossible to swap two values of compatible types and can be in any order. Concept explained in
[TestcontainersConfiguration.kt](../../test/support/TestcontainersConfiguration.kt.md#testconfigurationproxybeanmethods--false).

The lambda is the same row mapper as in `findAll` (see [the lambda](#mapping-each-row-the-lambda)).
`.query{` without a space is legal, and it formats the same.

### `singleOrNull`: zero or one row

```kotlin
// Why: The list singleOrNull below, we did this over the Java optional so we can stay within kotlin. We wont have more than one entry in the list because sku_id is the primary key so it is unique.
        .list().singleOrNull()
```

**Kotlin (`singleOrNull`):** a standard-library function on any `List`. It returns the only
element if the list has exactly one, and `null` otherwise:

| List | `singleOrNull()` | `single()` | `firstOrNull()` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `[]` | `null` | throws `NoSuchElementException` | `null` |
| `[a]` | `a` | `a` | `a` |
| `[a, b]` | **`null`** | throws `IllegalArgumentException` | `a` |

Note the last row: with two elements, `singleOrNull()` returns `null` silently. It doesn't
throw. So if two rows could ever match, the SKU would be reported as missing. That can't happen here
for the reason in the `// Why:` comment: `sku_id` is the primary key, so the database never holds two
rows with the same SKU. As with `findAll`, the migration's constraints are what make the Kotlin code
correct.

**Why not `JdbcClient`'s own `.optional()`:** the query spec also has `.optional()`, which returns a
Java `Optional<InventoryItem>`. Kotlin code would then convert it with `.orElse(null)` or
`.getOrNull()`. `.list().singleOrNull()` gets `InventoryItem?` directly, and a nullable type is the
Kotlin way to say "maybe absent". `.single()` was ruled out because it throws on no rows, and no rows
is a normal answer here.

**Kotlin (why the return type works):** `.list()` returns `List<InventoryItem>` (non-null items,
thanks to the lambda), and `singleOrNull()` on a `List<T>` returns `T?`. That gives
`InventoryItem?`, which matches the declared return type.

## Check your understanding

- What does `@Repository` do that `@Import(InventoryRepository::class)` does in the test? Why does the running app need the annotation?
- Where does the `JdbcClient` passed to the constructor come from? Why is there no `@Autowired`?
- Why is `jdbcClient` a `private val` rather than a plain constructor parameter or a `var`?
- What is the difference between the KDoc above `findAll` and the `// Why:` comment? Who reads each one, and where?
- Why does `query(InventoryItem::class.java)` produce `List<InventoryItem?>`, while the lambda produces `List<InventoryItem>`?
- What would the API return if `ORDER BY sku_id` were removed? Would the test notice every time?
- Why is it `getString("sku_id")` and not `getString("skuId")`?
- The expression body has no `return`. What makes that allowed?
- If `sku_id` could be NULL in the database, what would happen at runtime, and where?
- The service calls `findBySkuId("x' OR '1'='1")`. What SQL reaches Postgres, and what comes back?
- If the primary key were dropped and two `widget` rows existed, what would `findBySkuId("widget")` return? What would the API answer?
- Why can the service call `findBySkuId(skuId).quantity` only after handling `null`? Which line of the service does that?

entries.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: small — keep workflows under 5 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

content.text:
That's a solid explanation. You covered all three pieces. Here are a few corrections and the parts the code doesn't show.

**1. Who "solves" the null case.** You said "we have to solve the null case for this function." The more precise version: `findBySkuId` doesn't solve the null case, it *reports* it. The `?` means the **caller** has to deal with it. The compiler won't let the service use `.quantity` on an `InventoryItem?` until it has handled `null`. That split is deliberate:

- The **repository** says "no row" by returning `null`. That's a normal answer to a lookup, not an error.
- The **service** decides what "no row" *means* for this endpoint, which is a 404. Later, the purchase endpoint will make the same lookup and may give a different answer.

Java comparison: every Java reference can be null and nothing warns you. Kotlin puts that information in the type itself. At runtime `InventoryItem?` is just a normal reference, with no wrapper object like `Optional`.

**2. What `.param` actually does.** You're right that it stops SQL injection. Here's how:
- `JdbcClient` rewrites `:skuId` into JDBC's `?` and runs a `PreparedStatement`.
- Postgres receives the SQL text first and parses it, and only then receives the value.
- Because the query's structure is fixed before the value arrives, a SKU like `x' OR '1'='1` can't change it. It's just a string that matches nothing.

Compare the version we avoided: `"... WHERE sku_id = '$skuId'"` pastes the value into the SQL text, and the attacker's quote closes yours. `:skuId` (named) instead of `?` (positional) is only for readability.

**3. A `singleOrNull` detail worth knowing for the interview.** It has three cases, not two:

| List | `singleOrNull()` | `single()` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `[]` | `null` | throws |
| `[a]` | `a` | `a` |
| `[a, b]` | **`null`**, silently | throws |

So if two rows ever matched, the SKU would look *missing* and no error would be raised. Your reasoning is what makes this safe: `sku_id` is the primary key, so two rows can't exist. The Kotlin code is correct *because of* the database constraint.

**4. Something you didn't mention:** the lambda uses **named arguments**, `InventoryItem(skuId = ..., quantity = ...)`, while `findAll` passes them by position. Both compile to the same call. Named arguments make it impossible to swap two values by accident.

---

Any questions about the repository before we move on?

**Check question:** a request comes in for `GET /inventory/widget`, but someone has dropped the primary key and the table now holds two `widget` rows. What does `findBySkuId("widget")` return, and what HTTP response would the client get?

It would look like the first sku is missing so we would go through our SkuNotFoundException flow. Which would be a bug. If for some reason we needed to change sku_id and not have it be the primary key we would need to rework our return for findBySkuId.

## Role

The project's first custom exception, written by Robert. It names a domain problem, "this SKU
doesn't exist", without saying anything about HTTP. The [service](../InventoryService.kt.md) throws
it when the [repository](../InventoryRepository.kt.md) finds no row. It passes through the
[controller](../InventoryController.kt.md) untouched, and
[InventoryExceptionHandler](InventoryExceptionHandler.kt.md) turns it into a `404` with a
`text/plain` body.

It lives in the `error` subpackage, which was Robert's proposal (2026-09-27): custom exceptions and
the handler that maps them sit together, apart from the controller → service → repository files.
The alternatives were a flat `inventory` package (the error types mixed in with the layers) and a
top-level `com.robertwoolbright.inventory.error` (shared by every feature, but this project has only one).

## Walkthrough

### The package

```kotlin
package com.robertwoolbright.inventory.inventory.error
```

**Kotlin:** the package matches the folder `inventory/error/`. The compiler doesn't require that,
but the Kotlin style guide recommends it (Java tooling expects it), and every file in this project
follows it. Code in the
parent `inventory` package must import this class, as the [service does](../InventoryService.kt.md#imports).

### The whole class in one line

```kotlin
/** Thrown when the database is queried with the SKU, but the result comes back as null. This is thrown at the service level and is mapped to a 404 by InventoryExceptionHandler. */
class SkuNotFoundException(skuId: String) : RuntimeException("SKU not found: $skuId")
```

**Kotlin (extending a class):** `: RuntimeException(...)` after the constructor means "extends
`RuntimeException`". It's Java's `extends RuntimeException` plus a `super(...)` call in one step. The
parentheses are the call to the superclass constructor, and they're required: Kotlin always makes you
say which superclass constructor runs. Java equivalent:

```java
public class SkuNotFoundException extends RuntimeException {
    public SkuNotFoundException(String skuId) {
        super("SKU not found: " + skuId);
    }
}
```

**Kotlin (a plain constructor parameter):** `skuId: String` has no `val` or `var`, so it is *only* a
constructor parameter, not a property. It can be used while the object is being built (here, in the
superclass call), and then it's gone. `exception.skuId` doesn't compile. Compare
[`private val` in the repository](../InventoryRepository.kt.md#a-spring-bean-with-constructor-injection),
which keeps the value as a field. The SKU survives only inside the message text, which is all the
handler needs.

**Kotlin (string templates):** `"SKU not found: $skuId"` inserts the value of `skuId` into the string.
It's Java's `"SKU not found: " + skuId`. For anything more than a plain name, use braces:
`"${item.skuId}"` or `"${skuId.uppercase()}"`. Without braces, `$item.skuId` would insert `item`
and then the literal text `.skuId`.

**Kotlin (no body):** the class has nothing of its own to add, so it needs no `{ }`
(see [class with no body](../../InventoryApplication.kt.md#springbootapplication-and-a-class-with-no-body)). The class is also `final` by default,
so nothing can extend it, which is fine for an exception this specific.

**Why `RuntimeException`:** Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so extending `Exception` wouldn't force
anyone to catch it either. `RuntimeException` still matters for two reasons:
- Java callers and readers see an unchecked exception, which is what it behaves like.
- Spring's `@Transactional` rolls back by default only for unchecked exceptions (`RuntimeException`
  and `Error`). There's no transaction on this read path yet, but if a later write throws this
  exception, the transaction will roll back without any extra configuration.

**Why a custom exception and not `ResponseStatusException`:** Spring's
`ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, ...)` would carry the status itself, which puts HTTP
into the service. A custom exception keeps HTTP out of it: the service says *what* went wrong, and the handler decides how
that looks over HTTP. The purchase endpoint will throw the same exception for a missing SKU, and
the same handler will map it. (`ResponseStatusException` also doesn't give a `text/plain` body by
default; see [the handler notes](InventoryExceptionHandler.kt.md#the-class-and-why-its-an-advice).)

**Contract:** the message `SKU not found: <skuId>` is the `404` body, word for word. The contract
gives no example, so the wording was Robert's choice (2026-09-27), with **no trailing period**: a
period right after the id would make it unclear where the id ends (the id `CW-1.` is possible).
`InventoryControllerTest` checks the exact text.

## Check your understanding

- What would `SkuNotFoundException("widget").message` return? Could it ever be `null`?
- Why doesn't `ex.skuId` compile? What one-word change would make it compile?
- `"SKU not found: $sku.id"`: what does this string contain if `sku.id` is `"W-1"`?
- Why does the class name say nothing about `404`?

# Walkthrough: GET /inventory

- Date: 2026-09-25
- Covers: cf86d35..b150acb (plus uncommitted: yes, note improvements made during this session)
- Files: V1__create_inventory.sql, InventoryController.kt, InventoryService.kt, InventoryRepository.kt,
  InventoryItem.kt (all written by Robert; he explained each first), InventoryRepositoryTest.kt,
  InventoryControllerTest.kt (written by Claude; Claude explained)

## Concepts covered

- Primary key = `UNIQUE` + `NOT NULL` + index; natural key; `TEXT` compares case-sensitively; `CHECK` as the oversell backstop.
- Flyway migrations are a chain of changes: a new column is `V2__...` with `ALTER TABLE`; editing an applied V1 fails startup with a checksum mismatch.
- `@RestController` = `@Controller` + `@ResponseBody`; Jackson writes the return value as JSON with property names as keys.
- Class-level `@RequestMapping` is a path prefix; `@GetMapping("/{skuId}")` would map to `GET /inventory/{skuId}`.
- Beans are singletons built once at startup, bottom-up through constructor injection; one object serves every request thread, so beans must be stateless.
- The controller doesn't sort: ordering comes from the repository's `ORDER BY sku_id` (by collation, not strictly A-Z).
- Expression bodies; no checked exceptions; why not catching the DB exception is honest (500, not a false `[]`); why the service layer exists.
- Missing `@Service` fails fast at startup ("required a bean of type ... that could not be found").
- `JdbcClient` chain: `.sql` stores SQL, `.query` stores the row recipe, `.list()` runs and collects.
- Lambdas return their last expression; `_` is an unused parameter; the row-mapper lambda fixes a compile-time type problem, not a data problem.
- `data class` generates `equals`/`hashCode`/`toString`/`copy`/`componentN`; `data` doesn't mean immutable, `val` does.
- `==` calls `equals` (value vs identity); `copy` returns a new object and leaves the original unchanged.
- Test slices vs full context: `@JdbcTest` (rollback per test) vs `@SpringBootTest` + MockMvc (`@BeforeEach` cleanup), `@Autowired constructor`, Kotlin MockMvc DSL, raw strings, `JsonCompareMode.STRICT`.

## Questions Robert asked

- None beyond the understanding checks; he asked to go file by file along the request path.

## Understanding checks

- New `created_at` column after V1 ran → "new V2 file" (right), but thought V2 recreates the table and the newest file is the source of truth. Clarified: migrations are changes like git commits (`ALTER TABLE`), the schema is the whole chain. Then answered correctly that editing V1 errors at startup.
- Two simultaneous requests: how many controllers? → first said two objects on two threads. Re-explained (one ticket window, many customers; identityHashCode experiment). Re-check answered correctly: one object regardless of threads. Clarified that `val`-only fields are what make it safe.
- Remove `@Service` → correct: startup fails with a bean error (self-corrected from "fails on request").
- Repository chain and lambda → partial: thought `_` drives iteration and that the lambda returns nothing. Re-explained with a `Book`/`.map` trace table; he then answered `{ book -> book.year }` gives 1965, 1815 (List<Int>) correctly.
- Owed from session 02: `InventoryItem("widget", 5) == InventoryItem("widget", 5)` → first said "error, same skuId" (confused with the DB primary key). Clarified `==` is an in-memory `equals`: true with `data`, false without. Then `copy` check: `a == b` false (right); first said `a.quantity` becomes 6, corrected to 5 (copy makes a new object); answered `b` = widget, 6 correctly.
- `WHERE quantity > 0` added to `findAll` → right on ordering (pass) and zero stock (fail); wrong on empty list (thought fail) and backstop (right result, wrong reason). Lesson: trace which code each test actually calls.
- Rename `skuId` → `sku` → said no test fails. Clarified: the STRICT JSON test fails (Jackson writes `"sku"`); 1 of 7.

## Follow-ups

- Folded into notes: migrations-as-changes (V1 notes), singleton/threads/stateless (controller notes), chain table + lambda return values + `.map` example + collation (repository notes), `==`/`copy`/`data` ≠ immutable (InventoryItem notes), predicting test failures (repository test notes), rename breaks the STRICT test (controller test notes).
- Revisit before the interview: singleton beans vs threads, and lambda return values. Both needed a second explanation.
- Optional exercises: the `identityHashCode` experiment; comment out `@Service` and run `.\gradlew.bat test` to read the startup error.
- Optional polish (Robert's call): `InventoryService` class KDoc wording.
## Questions Robert asked

- Q: Wouldn't you need to update application.yml with the production database info?
  A: No. Spring layers property sources; environment variables (set by the infrastructure) override
  application.yml, so the repo never holds environment-specific values or passwords.
- Q: So environment variables are set at the infrastructure level and the service just reads them?
  A: Yes. Whatever launches the process sets them (k8s Deployment + Secret, ECS task definition,
  `docker run -e`, systemd). `.env` files are a local convenience and are gitignored.
- Q: Seth (Nuuly architect) said they chose Spring over Micronaut because environment-variable
  handling across environments was painful and a related bug kept them out of production for
  3 days. Does that relate, and is it a real advantage despite Micronaut's faster startup?
  A: It relates directly to config layering. Possible Micronaut culprits (speculative): automatic
  environment detection, looser env-var-to-property mapping, compile-time decisions. Startup speed
  matters most for serverless/scale-from-zero; predictability matters constantly. Suggested asking
  Seth which mechanism it was rather than claiming to know.
- (Environment) `./gradlew bootRun` failed with "JAVA_HOME is not set": VS Code was opened before
  Java was installed, so its terminals have a stale environment. Fix: restart VS Code fully.

## Understanding checks

- Splitting into modules: which file changes? → settings.gradle.kts with `include(...)`. Correct.
- Remove `plugin.spring`, add `@Transactional`: what breaks? → Correct on final vs open, but said a
  final class is "immutable". Clarified final ≠ immutable, that proxies wrap method calls, and that a
  final *method* fails silently. Added to the build notes.
- `import org.postgresql.PGConnection` with `runtimeOnly`? → "a dependency issue". Sharpened: it
  fails to *compile* (not on the compile classpath); `runtimeOnly` enforces the java.sql-only design.
- `@Nullable` + `result.length` with and without `-Xjsr305=strict`? → Correct. Added: without the flag
  it's only a warning; showed `?.` and `?:`.
- How does bootRun know the DB without application.yml settings? → "it's all in compose.yaml".
  Mostly right; the port comes from Docker, not the file.
- Deploy to db.example.com without editing files? → Unsure. Re-explained with property source
  precedence and relaxed binding; added to the application.yml notes. Follow-up
  (CLI vs env vs yml) → "cli-wins", correct.
- Controller in sibling package `com.robertwoolbright.web`? → "won't be found". Correct; added that the
  symptom is a silent 404 with no startup error.
- Who starts/stops the test container? → Spring, on bean creation / context close. Correct; added that
  with caching that means end of test run, and Ryuk as a safety net.
- Why keep `contextLoads`? → startup issues: dependencies, config, migrations. Correct; added that
  slices never assemble the full app.

## Follow-ups

- Restart VS Code so terminals see JAVA_HOME and Docker, then try the experiments:
  `docker ps` during bootRun; `$env:SPRING_APPLICATION_NAME = "hello-override"`; comment out
  `@Import` in InventoryApplicationTests and predict the failure.

# Interview prep

Questions a reviewer might ask in the follow-up interview, with short answers I should be able to
give out loud. Answers are folded: try each question first, then open it to check.

New questions are added during walkthroughs when a topic looks interview-worthy. Longer
explanations live in the [study notes](notes/README.md); each answer links to them.

## Design and failure modes

### What happens if two rows ever share the same SKU?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

`findBySkuId` ends in `.list().singleOrNull()`. With two rows, `singleOrNull()` returns `null`
without throwing. The service then throws `SkuNotFoundException`, and the client gets
**404 "SKU not found: widget"** for a SKU that actually exists twice. That's a silent bug: the API
gives a wrong answer and nothing is logged.

It can't happen today because `sku_id` is the **primary key**, so Postgres rejects a second
`widget` row. The Kotlin code is correct *because of* the database constraint. Keeping the primary
key is the real fix.

If `sku_id` ever stopped being unique, the lookup would need reworking:
- **`.single()`** throws on two rows, so the bug would surface loudly as a 500 instead of a false 404.
  But it also throws on **zero** rows, which is the normal "not found" case, so on its own it would
  turn every missing SKU into a 500.
- A version that handles both cases: `val rows = ...list()`, then `null` when `rows` is empty,
  the item when there's one, and an error (such as `IllegalStateException`) when there are more.
- Which row is "right" is a data question, not a code question, so a duplicate should fail, not be
  picked arbitrarily with `firstOrNull()`.

| List | `singleOrNull()` | `single()` | `firstOrNull()` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `[]` | `null` | throws | `null` |
| `[a]` | `a` | `a` | `a` |
| `[a, b]` | **`null`**, silently | throws | `a`, silently |

Notes: [InventoryRepository.kt, `singleOrNull`](notes/main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md#singleornull-zero-or-one-row)
</details>

### Why does the repository return `null` for a missing SKU instead of throwing?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

"No row" is a normal answer to a lookup, not a failure. The repository only reports what the table
holds. The **service** decides what a missing row means for each endpoint: `GET /inventory/{skuId}`
turns it into a 404, and the purchase endpoint can make its own decision. The `?` in
`InventoryItem?` forces every caller to handle the missing case, because the compiler won't let them
use `.quantity` until they have.

Notes: [InventoryRepository.kt, nullable return type](notes/main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md#findbyskuid-a-nullable-return-type)
</details>

### How do you prevent SQL injection?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

The SKU comes straight from the URL, so it's untrusted. The query uses a named parameter,
`WHERE sku_id = :skuId`, bound with `.param("skuId", skuId)`. `JdbcClient` runs it as a JDBC
`PreparedStatement`: Postgres parses the SQL first and receives the value separately, so the value
can never change the query's structure. `x' OR '1'='1` is just a string that matches no SKU.

Building the SQL with a string template (`"... WHERE sku_id = '$skuId'"`) would paste the value
into the SQL text, and the attacker's quote would close ours.

Notes: [InventoryRepository.kt, binding the parameter](notes/main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md#binding-the-parameter-and-mapping-the-row)
</details>

### What happens if the database is down during `GET /inventory`?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

`JdbcClient` throws a `DataAccessException`. Nothing catches it, so Spring returns a 500. That's
the honest answer: catching it and returning `[]` would tell the client "you have no stock" when
the truth is "we don't know".

Notes: [InventoryService.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryService.kt.md)
</details>

## Kotlin

### What does the `?` in `InventoryItem?` mean, and how is it different from Java's `Optional`?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

`InventoryItem?` is its own type, "an item or `null`", and the compiler keeps it apart from
`InventoryItem`. You can't call `.quantity` on it, return it where an `InventoryItem` is expected,
or pass it along, until you've handled `null` (`?.`, `?:`, an `if` check, or `!!`).

In Java any reference can be null and nothing warns you; `Optional` is an opt-in wrapper object.
Kotlin puts the information in the type at no runtime cost: an `InventoryItem?` is a normal
reference with no wrapper.

Notes: [InventoryRepository.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md#findbyskuid-a-nullable-return-type)
</details>

### Why is the row mapper a lambda and not `query(InventoryItem::class.java)`?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

The class-based version didn't compile: Spring 7 declares it as "each row might map to null", so
Kotlin saw `List<InventoryItem?>`. The lambda keeps its own return type, and it always builds a
real `InventoryItem`, so the list is `List<InventoryItem>`. It's a compile-time fix; the data was
never actually null. It's also more explicit about which column goes into which property.

Notes: [InventoryRepository.kt, the lambda](notes/main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md#mapping-each-row-the-lambda)
</details>

### What does `data class` give you, and does it make the class immutable?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

It generates `equals`, `hashCode`, `toString`, `copy` and `componentN` from the constructor
properties. So `InventoryItem("widget", 5) == InventoryItem("widget", 5)` is `true` (value
equality, because `==` calls `equals`). It does **not** make the class immutable: `val` does.
`copy` returns a new object and leaves the original unchanged.

Notes: [InventoryItem.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryItem.kt.md)
</details>

## Spring

### Two requests arrive at the same time. How many controller objects are there?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

One. Beans are singletons, built once at startup through constructor injection, bottom-up
(repository → service → controller). Every request thread shares the same object. That's safe
because the beans are **stateless**: they only hold `val` references to other beans, never
per-request data.

Notes: [InventoryController.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryController.kt.md)
</details>

### What happens if you remove `@Service` from `InventoryService`?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

The app fails at **startup**, not on the first request: the controller's constructor needs an
`InventoryService` bean and none exists ("required a bean of type ... that could not be found").
Beans are created at startup, so missing dependencies fail fast.

Notes: [InventoryService.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryService.kt.md)
</details>

### How would you deploy to a different database without changing any files?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

Set environment variables such as `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL`. Spring layers property sources, and
environment variables override `application.yml`, so the repo never holds per-environment values
or passwords. Whatever launches the process (Kubernetes, ECS, `docker run -e`) sets them.
Command-line arguments beat environment variables, which beat the yml.

Notes: [application.yml](notes/main/resources/application.yml.md)
</details>

## Database and migrations

### You need a new `created_at` column. What do you do?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

Add a new migration, `V2__add_created_at.sql`, with `ALTER TABLE`. Migrations are a chain of
changes, like commits; the schema is the whole chain. Editing `V1` after it has run makes Flyway
fail at startup with a checksum mismatch.

Notes: [V1__create_inventory.sql](notes/main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_inventory.sql.md)
</details>
